title: Exclusive caching contract across guest, hypervisor and database buffer pool
idea: Stack 'no application changes' with 'no new hardware': the only lever left is redundancy between layers. A virtio 'ownership ring' lets the database, guest kernel and hypervisor announce which file blocks each holds, so every block lives in exactly one layer like an exclusive victim cache: when the DB buffer pool evicts a page it is demoted into the guest/host page cache instead of discarded, and lower layers drop any block an upper layer owns.
why: File-backed data on virtualized database hosts is commonly cached 2-3 times (DB pool + guest page cache + host page cache); exclusivity frees ~30-60% of that DRAM with zero hardware or app change.

title: Range-translation MMU deletes page tables for huge shared mappings
idea: Stack 'no page-table memory' with 'no extra TLB misses': add a 32-entry range TLB plus an in-memory range table of (base, limit, offset) entries, and have the OS eagerly allocate physically contiguous extents for big anonymous and shared mappings. Where 4 KB mappings are forced (fork-heavy, fine-grained protection), each of hundreds of processes mapping a 512 GB shared region spends ~1 GB on PTEs; one range entry replaces all of it.
why: Page-table memory can reach 10-50% of DRAM on fork-heavy shared-memory database/analytics servers; range translation removes it and also cuts page-walk energy.

title: Receiver-granted transport collapses per-socket buffers into one shared pool
idea: Stack 'no switch changes' with 'full 400G line rate': instead of auto-tuning every TCP socket's send/receive buffers to several MB, receivers issue byte grants (Homa-style) so total in-flight data per host is capped near one bandwidth-delay product (~2-5 MB at 400G, 10 us RTT). All sockets draw from a single shared host buffer pool, and unsent data stays in application memory via zero-copy rather than kernel buffers.
why: Front-end, proxy and storage servers with 100k+ connections spend tens of GB on kernel socket buffers; capping in-flight bytes per host cuts network-buffer DRAM 10-100x.

title: Direct NVMe-to-HBM weight loading retires the 'host RAM twice HBM' rule
idea: Stack 'host DRAM at most 1/8 of GPU HBM' with 'model cold start under 10 s': store checkpoints pre-sharded in each GPU's native tensor layout across striped NVMe and load them with GPUDirect-Storage DMA (O_DIRECT, bypassing the page cache) straight into HBM, with only a tiny host bounce ring for metadata. Hosts no longer keep a full host-RAM copy of the weights for fast restarts.
why: 8-GPU inference servers typically carry 1-2 TB DDR5 mostly to stage and cache weights; 128-256 GB suffices, a 5-10x host-DRAM cut per server.

title: Retrofit retrieval so facts live on flash, not in parameters
idea: Stack 'the resident model must fit in 8 GB' with 'factual recall of a 70B model': freeze a 3-8B decoder and train lightweight chunked cross-attention layers (RETRO-fitting) that read neighbour passages from a 1-2 TB text-and-embedding datastore on NVMe via a disk-resident ANN index. Encyclopedic knowledge moves out of DRAM/HBM-resident weights into flash and can be updated without retraining.
why: Cuts resident parameter memory ~10x for knowledge-heavy workloads (70B to 7B in HBM), shifting the bulk into NAND at ~1/20 the cost per bit.

title: Live-price five-minute rule sets every cache's eviction horizon
idea: Stack 'no new hardware' with 'caches must react to the 4x DRAM price spike by themselves': each buffer pool computes Gray's break-even interval T = (pages per MB of DRAM / accesses per second per NVMe) x (NVMe price / DRAM price per MB) from live procurement prices and measured device IOPS, and evicts to NVMe any object whose inter-reference time exceeds T. With 4x DRAM prices and million-IOPS NVMe, T falls from minutes to seconds.
why: Turns a price shock into automatic footprint cuts: OLTP and caching buffer pools shrink ~2-4x when T drops ~10x, at small latency cost on NVMe.

title: Type-segregated pages make per-object headers implicit
idea: Stack 'unchanged bytecode' with 'unchanged pointer width' (so pointer compression is off the table): the allocator places all objects of one class in dedicated 64 KB 'big bag of pages' spans, so the class pointer is read from span metadata at (address >> 16) while mark, lock and hash bits move to side bitmaps and a sparse lock table. The 12-16 byte per-object header disappears.
why: Small-object-heavy JVM/.NET/JS heaps spend 20-40% of bytes on headers; implicit headers cut heap DRAM ~1.3-1.6x on top of existing pointer compression.

title: Peak-liveness operator ordering with interval-coloring buffer reuse
idea: Stack 'no recomputation' with 'no offload': the only freedom left is order and placement, so the ML compiler searches topological orders of the graph (dynamic programming over frontiers with pruning) to minimize maximum live tensor bytes, then packs tensor lifetimes into one arena by interval-graph coloring with in-place aliasing of elementwise ops.
why: Branchy graphs (U-Nets, diffusion, multimodal encoders, MoE routing) carry 1.5-3x peak activation slack under default execution order; recovered with zero extra FLOPs or traffic.

title: One DRAM replica plus flash followers primed by hot-set manifests
idea: Stack 'three-way durability' with 'only one copy in DRAM': in-memory stores keep the leader in DRAM while followers apply the replication stream into an NVMe LSM tree; the leader piggybacks a periodic hot-key manifest (top keys by access frequency) so a promoted follower bulk-prefetches its hot set and regains full hit rate within seconds of failover.
why: Replicated in-memory tiers (caches, feature stores, session stores) hold 2-3 full DRAM copies; this cuts DRAM to ~1.1x of the data with seconds-scale recovery.

title: Operate directly on wire-format buffers; never build object graphs
idea: Stack 'no deserialization step' with 'keep a typed API': RPC and storage layers adopt offset-addressed in-place formats (Cap'n Proto/FlatBuffers-style) with generated accessors that read fields straight from the received byte buffer, and handlers pass buffer slices downstream instead of materialized objects.
why: In Java/Python services, deserialized object graphs are 3-10x larger than wire bytes and dominate request-path heap; in-place access cuts request memory 2-5x.

title: Deploy-time service fusion compiles co-located microservices into one process
idea: Stack 'developers keep writing separate microservices' with 'only one runtime per host': a deploy-time linker finds services the scheduler co-locates and compiles them into one process with in-process typed calls replacing RPC, sharing one heap, connection pool, TLS/config cache and library copy, while keeping per-service fault domains via supervisors.
why: Each JVM/Python/Node microservice carries a 150-500 MB baseline plus duplicated caches and serialization buffers; fusing ~10 services per host cuts host memory 3-5x.

title: Traffic-profiled vocabulary trimming shrinks embeddings and LM head
idea: Stack 'no retraining' with 'no quality loss on served languages': log the token IDs a deployment's real traffic uses for a week, keep those covering 99.99% plus the byte-fallback set, and physically delete all other rows of the input embedding and output head, remapping tokenizer IDs.
why: Multilingual 256k-vocab models spend 10-30% of small-model weights on embeddings/head; trimming to ~32k cuts those 8x and total weight memory 10-25% for single-region deployments.

title: Fleet audit converts static memory reservations into lazy commits
idea: Stack 'no application rewrite' with 'no overcommit risk': a fleet scanner finds statically reserved but untouched DRAM (boot-time hugetlbfs pools, DPDK mempools, crashkernel regions, JVMs with Xms=Xmx plus AlwaysPreTouch) and swaps each for a lazy equivalent: on-demand huge-page promotion, firmware-assisted dump instead of a reserved capture kernel, and mempools grown on demand.
why: Static reservations commonly strand 5-15% of server DRAM fleetwide; reclaiming them is configuration and kernel work only.

title: OOM-as-migration lets schedulers allocate predicted, not requested, memory
idea: Stack 'jobs get only their predicted median footprint' with 'zero OOM kills': when a container nears its cgroup limit, the node agent freezes it, takes a CRIU checkpoint to local NVMe and restores it on a host with free memory (or raises the limit if the host has room), so safety padding in memory requests becomes unnecessary.
why: Batch, HPC and Kubernetes memory requests average 2-3x actual use; a transparent escape hatch raises cluster memory utilization 1.5-2.5x.

title: bf16 weights with 8-bit compensation bytes replace FP32 master copy
idea: Stack 'no FP32 master weights' with 'mixed-precision-equivalent convergence': keep weights in bf16 plus one 8-bit Kahan compensation byte per parameter that accumulates each update's rounding error and is folded into the bf16 value when it exceeds half an ulp.
why: Adam mixed-precision training uses ~16 B/parameter; replacing the 4 B FP32 master with 1 B cuts training-state memory ~19% at no accuracy cost.

title: Database cracking builds index only where queries actually probe
idea: Stack 'no full secondary indexes in DRAM' with 'no full-table scans': each range query partially reorders the column around its predicate bounds (cracking) and a tiny tree records cracked-piece boundaries, so index structure accumulates only over value ranges real queries touch, and cold pieces are merged back.
why: In-memory OLTP/HTAP engines often devote 30-100% of DRAM to B-tree secondary indexes; for skewed workloads cracking cuts that 5-20x.

title: NIC page-fault support unpins RDMA and GPU-registered host memory
idea: Stack 'keep zero-copy RDMA/GPU DMA' with 'no pinned memory': use on-demand paging in the NIC/IOMMU (ATS/PRI page requests) so registered regions stay pageable and reclaimable, with the NIC faulting pages in on first DMA; libraries register whole address spaces instead of pre-pinning per-connection buffer pools.
why: Pinned registration pools (NCCL, RDMA verbs, CUDA pinned host buffers) strand 10-30% of DRAM on ML and storage hosts; pageable registration returns it.

title: Watermark-provable state expiry for exact streaming joins
idea: Stack 'exact results' with 'bounded state': a query rewriter converts unbounded stream joins into interval joins by inferring event-time bounds from data contracts (e.g. payment within 24 h of order) and uses watermarks to prove a key can never match again, deleting its state at that instant rather than at a padded TTL.
why: Stream processors hold unbounded or TTL-padded join state (TB-scale on large pipelines); provable expiry cuts state DRAM 5-50x with no approximation.

title: Runtime collection morphing swaps data-structure implementations per allocation site
idea: Stack 'no source changes' with 'no programmer effort': the JIT profiles each allocation site's collections (size, operation mix) and transparently rebinds them: a HashMap that never exceeds 8 entries becomes a packed array map, a never-mutated list becomes an exact-size frozen array, a boxed Integer list becomes a primitive int array, dispatched through polymorphic inline caches.
why: Collection overhead (empty tables, load-factor slack, boxing) is 30-60% of many enterprise heaps; site-specific morphing cuts heap 1.3-2x automatically.

title: Speculative decoding sized by Little's law shrinks concurrent KV
idea: Stack 'no KV compression or eviction' with 'same throughput': since KV memory = request rate x time-in-system x KV per request, cut time-in-system: a small draft model or prompt n-gram lookup proposes 4-8 tokens verified in one pass, finishing each request 2-3x sooner, and the scheduler is retuned to hold proportionally fewer concurrent sequences.
why: At fixed QPS the concurrent KV footprint falls 2-3x, so the same service needs 2-3x less HBM for KV; reframes speculation as a capacity tool rather than a latency tool.

title: Retrofit pretrained models to mostly sliding-window attention layers
idea: Stack 'keep the pretrained checkpoint' with 'long context but bounded KV': a short continued-training run converts 5 of every 6 layers to 4k sliding-window attention while every sixth stays global (interleaved local/global), so windowed layers keep a fixed ring buffer of KV regardless of context length.
why: At 128k context, KV memory drops ~5x (1/6 of layers full-length + 5/6 x 4k/128k), multiplying concurrent long sessions per GPU.

title: Unikernel function images shrink per-tenant microVMs from 256 MB to 8 MB
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out new silicon and favors deleting whole software layers: a 4-person team (~$800k) builds a toolchain that links each serverless function with a library OS (Unikraft-style: no init, shell, page cache or package manager) into a single-address-space microVM booting in 8-16 MB fixed memory, piloted on a 200-host FaaS cluster.
why: Per-tenant memory falls ~15-30x (128-256 MB to ~8 MB), so the same tenant count needs ~1/15 the DRAM; embodied fab ultrapure water scales with bits bought, and fewer hosts cut cooling water, giving >10x water reduction for the FaaS tier.

title: Stateless load balancers carry flow state encrypted inside connection IDs
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) favors deleting state rather than shrinking it: an L4 load balancer/NAT writes each flow's backend ID and port mapping, AES-encrypted and MAC'd, into the QUIC connection ID (TCP falls back to consistent hashing with state kept only for rare remapped flows), so any LB instance rebuilds the mapping from the packet itself; ~$600k builds an open XDP/eBPF implementation and a 10-site pilot.
why: Replicated per-flow tables (tens of GB per LB node) go to near zero, a >100x DRAM cut for the LB tier; the boxes shrink to small air/dry-cooled nodes, so that tier's embodied and operating water drop >10x.

title: Feistel-cipher permutation replaces shuffle buffers in training data loaders
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): a 2-person, ~$400k open-source loader generates each epoch's uniform shuffle on the fly with a keyed 4-round Feistel network over record indices (cycle-walking for non-power-of-two sizes) and issues random NVMe/object-store reads via io_uring, so neither shuffle buffers nor full in-RAM dataset caches are needed.
why: Training hosts often carry 0.5-2 TB RAM mainly for dataset caches and shuffle buffers; ~64 GB suffices, a 10-30x host-DRAM cut with matching embodied-water savings and lower host power (less cooling water).

title: Rolling-shutter-synchronous inference consumes camera rows as they read out
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): restructure a detection CNN into a row-streaming dataflow in which each layer keeps only a k-row line buffer and is clocked by the sensor's rolling-shutter readout, so a 4K frame is consumed as it leaves the sensor and only detections reach DRAM; a ~$700k FPGA-on-sensor-board prototype targets multi-camera vehicles and city cameras.
why: Frame buffers (hundreds of MB to GB across 8-12 automotive cameras) shrink to <10 MB on-chip SRAM, a >20x DRAM cut; DRAM-free passive-cooled edge modules also avoid shipping video to evaporatively cooled data centers, cutting water >10x.

title: Shallow-buffer switches plus NIC timing-wheel pacing replace HBM-buffered routers
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out building new switch ASICs, so change traffic instead: enable per-flow hardware pacing (timing-wheel queues in existing SmartNICs) on all hosts so aggregate traffic arrives smooth, then prove on a 64-rack testbed (~$900k incl. leased gear) that on-chip-SRAM-only switches match deep-buffer HBM switches on loss and tail latency, and publish a procurement spec.
why: Deep-buffer switches carry 8-16 GB HBM per ASIC; shallow switches delete those bits entirely (>100x fewer buffer bits) and ~20-30% of switch power, so the network tier's embodied fab water falls >10x.

title: Reversible coupling adapters invert activations during fine-tuning backward pass
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): wrap each block of an existing open model in an additive coupling (y1 = x1 + F(x2), y2 = x2 + G(y1)) initialized from the pretrained block weights and healed by brief continued training; backward reconstructs each layer's input exactly from its output, so stored activation memory is constant in depth. ~$500k ships the library and validates it on 7-70B models.
why: Activation memory falls by roughly the layer count (30-80x), so a 70B fine-tune fits on one 8-GPU node instead of 4-8; ~4-8x less HBM/DRAM provisioned plus fewer cooled node-hours approaches 10x less water per fine-tune.

title: Per-node eBPF proxy retires the one-sidecar-per-pod service mesh
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): replace per-pod Envoy sidecars (50-150 MB each) with an in-kernel eBPF L4 data path plus one shared per-node L7 proxy that multiplexes all pods' mTLS and routing; ~$600k funds automated migration tooling and a 2,000-pod pilot.
why: At ~100 pods per node, mesh memory drops from ~10 GB to ~0.5 GB (~20x); freed DRAM lets clusters shrink, cutting the mesh's embodied DRAM water >10x and node cooling water with it.

title: Shim runs unmodified Electron apps on the shared system webview
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): a compatibility layer intercepts Electron's BrowserWindow and Node APIs and maps them onto the OS's already-resident WebView (WebView2/WKWebView/WebKitGTK) plus one shared Node helper daemon, so each app stops bundling and running its own Chromium; ~$800k for 5 engineers to cover the top 50 Electron apps.
why: Each Electron app idles at 300-800 MB; on the shared engine most fall to 30-80 MB (~10x), so laptops and VDI hosts ship with far less DRAM, a ~10x cut in embodied DRAM water per desktop session.

title: Incremental view maintenance replaces in-memory OLAP for fixed dashboards
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): most BI dashboards rerun the same queries, so compile them once into incrementally maintained dataflows (DBSP/differential-dataflow style) that update MB-sized aggregates from change streams instead of holding TB-scale tables in in-memory OLAP clusters; ~$700k funds a SQL-to-IVM compiler and three customer pilots.
why: Memory held drops from the size of the data to the size of the answers plus join state (often 10-1000x); retiring in-memory OLAP clusters cuts embodied DRAM water and their evaporative cooling load >10x.

title: DIMM-less HBM-only nodes enable dry-cooled warm-water racks
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out new cooling plants, so remove the component that forces air and chillers: run memory-lean workloads on CPUs with on-package HBM in HBM-only mode with no DIMMs, so every heat source sits under a cold plate fed at ~45 C and heat leaves via dry coolers year-round; ~$900k funds a 40-node pilot plus a footprint audit that moves workloads with <100 GB/socket working sets onto them.
why: Removes air-cooled DIMMs (the main blocker to 100% liquid capture) and cuts DRAM per node ~8x (1 TB DDR5 to 128 GB HBM); evaporative cooling water goes to near zero (>10x) and embodied DRAM water falls ~8x.

title: Footprint-aware GPU slicing packs long-tail models into partitions
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): a scheduler profiles each served model's real HBM footprint and packs long-tail models (most under 10 GB) into MIG/MPS partitions with enforced memory limits instead of granting each a whole 80-192 GB GPU; ~$500k builds the packer and an SLO-aware admission controller for a 500-GPU fleet.
why: Long-tail serving fleets often use <15% of their HBM; packing 6-10 models per GPU cuts HBM bought for that tier ~7-10x, and fewer GPUs cut cooling water proportionally.

title: DRAM-less baseboard controller runs from on-chip SRAM and XIP flash
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): port BMC management firmware from embedded Linux (needing 512 MB-1 GB DDR) to a Rust RTOS that executes in place from QSPI NOR and keeps all state in 2-4 MB on-chip SRAM while still exposing Redfish/IPMI; ~$800k for firmware plus an open reference BMC board.
why: Deletes 0.5-1 GB DRAM per server (100% of BMC DRAM across millions of servers) plus its standby power; the BMC subsystem's embodied water falls >10x.

title: Pay-only-for-10x bounties on memory hogs in top open-source packages
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out funding hardware, so buy leverage: a $1M fund pays bounties only for merged patches that cut a widely deployed component's resident footprint by at least 10x on a public benchmark (default buffer sizes, eager caches, per-thread arenas), verified by reproducible CI measurement and weighted by install base.
why: The 10x threshold forces architectural fixes rather than tuning; one popular package fixed across millions of hosts frees PB-scale DRAM, a 10x embodied-water cut for each fixed component at ~1000x better leverage per dollar than buying DRAM.

title: Automated stackless conversion of thread-per-connection servers
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): a source-to-source compiler turns blocking thread-per-connection C/C++/Java server code into stackless state machines (CPS transform at each blocking call, live variables hoisted into a per-connection frame), so 100k connections need 100k small frames instead of 100k threads with user stacks and 16 KB kernel stacks; ~$700k for the transformer and two production pilots.
why: Per-connection memory falls from ~64-256 KB to ~1-4 KB, >20x for connection-heavy servers; fewer hosts for the same connections cut embodied and cooling water >10x for that tier.

title: Out-of-core vectorized engine on one NVMe box replaces in-memory clusters
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): migrate Spark-style in-memory ETL onto a single-node morsel-driven vectorized engine that spills grace-hash joins and sorts to NVMe RAID at 50+ GB/s with a fixed 64-128 GB RAM budget; ~$600k funds a translation layer for existing PySpark/SQL jobs and a benchmark-backed migration service.
why: Clusters provision 3-5x the data size in JVM heap across many nodes; out-of-core execution needs ~1-5% of data size in RAM, a 10-50x DRAM cut, and one box replaces 10-20 nodes, cutting cooling water likewise.

title: Distill narrow LLM tasks into weighted finite-state transducers
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): for high-volume narrow tasks (intent routing, PII redaction, field extraction), have the LLM label millions of logged and synthetic inputs, then induce a weighted finite-state transducer plus a small boosted-tree fallback that runs on CPU in a few MB, escalating only low-confidence inputs to the LLM; ~$500k builds the induction pipeline.
why: Replaces tens of GB of resident weights and KV per replica with MB-scale automata for 80-95% of that traffic (>100x memory cut); CPU-only serving needs no liquid or evaporative cooling, so water drops >10x.

title: Offline materialized head-query answers remove most online model memory
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): mine query logs for the head of the distribution (e.g. top 5M normalized queries covering 70-90% of traffic), generate answers in an offline batch at a dry-cooled site, and serve them from an SSD key-value store with freshness-triggered regeneration, so only tail queries reach live GPU serving; ~$400k builds the normalizer, batch pipeline and invalidation.
why: Live serving capacity (HBM/DRAM for weights and KV) shrinks with the head share, ~5-10x; batch generation runs at full utilization in dry-cooled facilities, so total water for the service falls ~10x.

title: Cohort-level targeting replaces per-user profile stores in ad bidding
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): real-time bidders keep per-user feature profiles for billions of IDs in DRAM; replace them with a few thousand cohort vectors, where each browser/device computes its cohort locally (Topics-API style) and sends only the cohort ID with the bid request; ~$800k pilot with one mid-size exchange.
why: Multi-TB replicated profile stores per region collapse to MB of cohort tables (>1000x DRAM cut for the bidder); retiring those clusters cuts embodied and cooling water far more than 10x, and improves privacy.

title: Water-utility rebates pay per verified gigabyte of DRAM avoided
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water) rules out building anything, so redirect existing money: a water utility in a data-center region runs a $1M pilot rebate (modeled on energy-efficiency rebates) paying operators per measured GB of installed DRAM retired or not purchased through footprint reduction, with an M&V protocol that counts embodied fab water plus operating cooling water and higher rates for 10x workload cuts.
why: Makes memory efficiency a water-conservation asset utilities already budget for; rebated projects must show 10x water reduction per workload, steering capital toward architectural memory cuts instead of DRAM purchases.

title: One game instance renders many players' views from shared assets
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): cloud gaming runs one full game process (8-16 GB of assets in RAM/VRAM) per player; instead, modify an open engine to host N sessions of the same title in one process with shared asset and world memory, rendering per-player viewports with separate input and encode streams; ~$700k for engine work and a 100-GPU pilot.
why: For co-located sessions of one title, memory per player falls from ~12 GB to ~1-2 GB (6-12x), cutting DRAM/VRAM bought and server count; embodied and cooling water fall ~10x per streamed session.

title: Closed-world AOT native images shrink JVM microservices tenfold
idea: Stack ($1M/24 mo) x (10x less water): compile JVM services ahead of time with closed-world reachability analysis (GraalVM native-image style), which drops the JIT compiler, code cache, unreachable classes and most class metadata; ~$500k funds an automated reflection-configuration inference tool and migration of 100 services.
why: Small JVM services idle at 200-500 MB RSS versus 20-60 MB as native images (~10x), cutting DRAM per pod and node count, for ~10x lower embodied DRAM water and fewer cooled hosts.

title: Tardigrade sugar-glass heaps: header-free vitrified regions for frozen object graphs
idea: A desiccated tardigrade swaps its water for trehalose glass. In the same way, a managed runtime 'vitrifies' object graphs that have survived N collections without a write: it moves them into a columnar glass region where each class's objects are struct-of-arrays rows, the class pointer and lock/hash word are stored once per block, and an object's identity is its row index. A write barrier 'rehydrates' any touched object back into the normal heap and leaves a forwarding entry.
why: Object headers (12-16 B) plus alignment make up 20-40% of small-object Java/.NET/Python heaps. Vitrifying the cold, immutable majority cuts managed-heap DRAM by ~15-30% without a compression codec.

title: Firn replay buffers: ice-core layer thinning for RL experience memory
idea: Replay buffers now keep every transition across millions of steps. Instead, experience is stored in age layers that compact like firn turning to ice: when a layer ages past a boundary it is cut 2x by stratified subsampling that keeps coverage of state-space clusters and high-TD-error transitions, so the retained count grows as O(log T). Sampling weights are rescaled by each layer's thinning factor so the gradient stays unbiased.
why: RL and robotics replay buffers reach 100s of GB of host DRAM per learner. Log-thinned layers cut that 10-50x at similar sample efficiency for long-horizon training.

title: Geode-fill allocator: size classes grown to each program's cavity
idea: Geode crystals grow to fit the cavity they have. Fleet heap profiles give each binary's exact allocation-size histogram, and a dynamic-programming solver picks the 60-90 size-class boundaries that minimize rounding slack for that histogram. The table is embedded at link time and loaded by a tcmalloc/jemalloc-style allocator in place of its generic geometric classes.
why: Generic size classes waste ~8-15% of the heap to internal fragmentation. Per-binary learned classes recover most of that, a few percent of fleet DRAM with no hardware change.

title: Endolith packing: tiny owned objects live in host struct padding pores
idea: Cryptoendolithic lichens live in the pores inside sandstone. A compiler pass emits a 'pore map' of each struct's padding and alignment holes. When it can prove that a small allocation (a refcount block, a small optional, a 4-8 B side record) is owned by a host object and dies with it, it places that allocation in the host's padding instead of on the heap.
why: C++/Rust heaps carry 5-15% padding plus 8-16 B of allocator overhead per small allocation. Colonizing the pores removes both for owned children, a ~3-8% heap cut.

title: Naked mole-rat switch: data structures change metabolism under memory hypoxia
idea: Naked mole-rats switch to fructose metabolism when oxygen runs out. Libraries ship paired fat/lean implementations (hash join vs sort-merge with spill, dense array vs roaring bitmap, open-address map at 50% load vs Swiss table at 95%), and each instance converts its representation in place when the kernel's PSI memory-pressure signal crosses a threshold, then converts back when pressure clears.
why: Hosts are sized for peak footprint. If every large structure can shrink 2-3x under pressure, machines can be sized near median footprint, ~20-30% less DRAM per host.

title: Tree-ring containers: grow by adding rings, never moving heartwood
idea: A tree adds a ring each year without moving the old wood. Growable arrays, deques and hash tables are rebuilt as ring segments of geometrically chosen sizes behind a tiny directory (Brodnik-style resizable arrays), so growth allocates only a new outer ring and never copies the old contents.
why: Doubling vectors waste ~25% on average and briefly need 3x the payload while they reallocate. Ring growth cuts the slack to O(sqrt n) and removes the copy peak that sets provisioned memory, ~10-25% for container-heavy services.

title: Intertidal stack harvesting: reclaim thread-stack pages exposed at low tide
idea: A runtime agent samples each thread's stack pointer and, like an ebb tide exposing the shore, releases (MADV_DONTNEED) the stack pages below the low-water mark seen over the last window, keeping a guard page to catch the next deep call. Pools of thousands of threads stop holding the commit from their deepest-ever recursion.
why: Services with 2-10k threads often carry 1-8 GB of committed but dead stack after rare deep call paths. Tidal harvesting returns most of it at negligible CPU cost.

title: Diagenetic B-trees: index nodes cement denser as sediment ages
idea: Buried sediment compacts and cements, falling from ~60% to ~10% porosity. In-memory B+trees and ART indexes track how recently each subtree took an insert. Once a subtree has gone a set period without one, a background pass rebuilds it at 100% fill with prefix-truncated keys, while the young, write-hot edge stays at the usual ~70% fill.
why: In-memory index nodes average ~65-70% fill, and indexes are often 30-50% of an in-memory database's footprint. Densifying the cold majority recovers ~25-30% of index DRAM.

title: Unconformity objects: store only the strata a record actually deposited
idea: A geological unconformity is a gap where layers were never laid down. A runtime splits each class into shapes keyed by which fields differ from their semantic default (null, empty, enum default, sentinel such as -1) and stores only the present fields plus a shape id. On the first write to an absent field, the object migrates to a wider shape.
why: Protobuf, ORM and DOM objects typically leave 50-80% of their fields unset. Shape-specialized layout cuts those object populations by 30-60%, and they are a large share of service heaps.

title: Gutless tube-worm GPU servers: retire the host-RAM-equals-2x-HBM rule
idea: Giant tube worms have no gut; their symbionts feed them directly. GPU servers ship with host DRAM about 2x their total HBM, mostly to stage weights, checkpoints and dataloader buffers. Route weight loads and checkpoints NVMe-to-HBM by peer DMA, decode input data on the GPU, and size host RAM for the OS and control plane only.
why: An 8-GPU node with ~1.1 TB of HBM usually ships 2 TB of DDR5. Cutting that to 256-512 GB frees ~1.5 TB per node, in the segment that is absorbing DRAM output.

title: Deep-biosphere slow lane: budget-planned batch jobs on 1/20 DRAM
idea: Subsurface microbes live on almost no energy and divide once in centuries. The query and data-pipeline planner gets a hard DRAM budget and a cost model in which time is the cheap resource, so it picks multi-pass external-memory algorithms and pebbling-optimal operator orders that run 3-10x longer in 5-10% of the memory. The result is sold as a cheap no-deadline slow lane.
why: Deadline-insensitive batch jobs hold much of analytics DRAM. A budgeted slow lane could free 30-50% of a cluster's batch memory for interactive work.

title: Pando page tables: one shared root system under thousands of processes
idea: The Pando aspen grove is one root system under ~47,000 trunks. When many processes map the same large region (inference workers sharing 200 GB of weights, Postgres backends sharing buffers), the kernel links a single shared page-table subtree into every process instead of building per-process PTEs for the same pages.
why: With 4 KB pages, 64 workers mapping 200 GB duplicate ~25 GB of page tables. Shared subtrees cut that ~64x and also speed attach and fork.

title: Grain-scale frame metadata: describe memory by grains, not atoms
idea: Petrologists describe rock by its mineral grains, not by each atom. The kernel's 64-byte descriptor for every 4 KB frame (struct page) is replaced by one descriptor per allocated extent (folio/memdesc), and per-frame state is kept only where an extent has been split.
why: Per-frame descriptors cost ~16 GB per TB of DRAM. Extent descriptors cut that to under 0.1%, giving back ~15 GB per TB host with no hardware change.

title: Conglomerate tensors: cement fragmented accelerator memory into one virtual block
idea: A conglomerate is loose pebbles cemented into one rock. The deep-learning caching allocator stops requiring contiguous physical HBM: it maps scattered free chunks into one contiguous virtual range with the GPU virtual-memory reserve/map/unmap APIs, so a large tensor can occupy holes that would otherwise be stranded.
why: Training and serving allocators strand 10-30% of HBM in fragments. Stitching recovers most of it, roughly one extra GPU's memory for every 5-8 GPUs.

title: Bioturbation shuffle: mix training data in place, no shuffle buffer
idea: Burrowing animals mix sediment layers where they lie. Training input pipelines drop their multi-GB shuffle buffers and instead walk a keyed Feistel-cipher permutation over record indices, reading shards in a block-randomized order that changes every epoch, so the randomness comes from index arithmetic rather than buffered samples.
why: Shuffle and prefetch buffers take tens to hundreds of GB of host DRAM per training node. Index-permutation shuffling cuts them to near zero with equivalent randomness.

title: Lyapunov-horizon feature stores: forget history beyond predictability limit
idea: Weather loses its predictability after about two weeks, however much past data is kept. For each user-history feature in recommendation and fraud stores, measure how its mutual information with the label decays with event age, then truncate that feature's in-memory window at its measured horizon (often hours for clicks, weeks for purchases) instead of a uniform 90-365 days.
why: Online feature stores and user-sequence caches use TB-scale DRAM for long, uniform windows. Per-feature horizons can cut 50-80% of that with no accuracy loss.

title: Salt-in parsing: services live inside encoded buffers, never deserialize
idea: Halophiles keep their cytoplasm as salty as the brine around them instead of spending energy to desalinate. Services likewise stop deserializing protobuf/Thrift/JSON into object trees and run generated accessors directly over the encoded buffer, decoding fields lazily and building offset tables on first access.
why: Deserialized object trees are 3-10x the wire size and are often a service's largest transient heap. Operating in place cuts request-path heap by 50-80%.

title: River-competence decoding: never lift pixels the consumer cannot carry
idea: A river's competence is the largest grain it can move. Image, video and point-cloud preprocessing decodes directly to the resolution the consumer needs (DCT-domain 1/2-1/8 scaled JPEG decode, wavelet subband truncation, decoding only the tiles in the region of interest), so full-resolution bitmaps never land in DRAM before a resize.
why: ML preprocessing and thumbnail fleets decode 12-48 MP images (48-190 MB of RGBA) only to shrink them below 1 MP. Competence decoding cuts per-worker buffers 10-60x.

title: Prescribed-burn transplants: periodic live-state rebirth into fresh processes
idea: A prescribed burn clears years of built-up fuel before it can cause disaster. A long-running service periodically forks a fresh seedling process, hands over only its reachable logical state (shared-memory serialization plus socket passing) and retires the old process, clearing allocator fragmentation, leaked native memory and bloated caches in one step.
why: Long-lived servers creep 10-30% above their true live footprint. Staggered transplants hold RSS near the live size, so the fleet can be provisioned at the lower level.

title: Varve-banded caches: store items in expiry-season layers, drop whole bands
idea: A lake varve lays down one band per season. Key-value caches place items into segments by expiry window, share timestamps and metadata across each segment, and drop a whole band when it expires, instead of tracking a TTL, LRU pointers and a free-list entry for every item.
why: Per-item metadata runs 40-60 B on 100-300 B values in memcached-class caches. Banded segments cut that overhead ~80% and evict expired-but-resident garbage promptly, for ~20-40% more items per GB.

title: Endospore imports: modules germinate only when their receptor symbol is touched
idea: A bacterial endospore germinates only when its receptors detect a specific nutrient. Python/JS/JVM services replace eager import trees with lazy module stubs that load code, constants and static tables only when one of the module's symbols is first touched. A fleet-collected 'germinant' profile prewarms the modules that are always used.
why: Large services import hundreds of modules and hold 200 MB-2 GB per process of code and data that is never used. Across many workers per host, lazy germination cuts RSS by 20-50%.

title: Delta-distributary DIMMs: many shallow channels built from Virginia-made dies
idea: A delta spreads a river over many shallow channels. Bandwidth-bound servers (HPC stencils, streaming analytics, CPU inference) must populate all 8-12 channels and so buy 512 GB-1 TB they never use. Build 8-16 GB full-bandwidth RDIMMs from mature-node dies made at Micron's Manassas, Virginia fab, assembled and tested on a domestic module line, and sell server configurations sized to bandwidth rather than capacity.
why: Cuts the DRAM bought per bandwidth-bound server 4-8x, and turns the lower density of U.S. mature-node dies into a non-issue because density is not what these servers need.

title: Iceland-spar buffer chip: one crystal, two images, one data copy
idea: Iceland spar calcite shows every object as two images. An on-DIMM buffer chip fabbed at GlobalFoundries Malta, NY (12LP) transposes 8x8-byte blocks on the fly, so one row-major copy of a table can also be streamed column-wise at near-full bandwidth. HTAP databases can then drop their second, columnar in-memory copy.
why: Dual-format in-memory databases keep both row and column copies, about 2x the footprint. One transposable copy saves ~40-50% of their DRAM, using logic on a mature U.S. node.

title: Icefish servers: Arizona SRAM-stacked nodes running small services without DRAM
idea: Antarctic icefish lost their hemoglobin because cold water carries enough oxygen. Intel 18A compute tiles (Arizona) are stacked by Foveros (Rio Rancho, New Mexico) onto SRAM base dies, giving ~1-2 GB of on-package SRAM per socket. Sidecars, proxies and serverless functions run in cache-as-RAM mode with no private DRAM pages; DRAM holds only shared read-only images and spill.
why: Millions of small instances each hold 0.5-4 GB of DRAM for working sets under 1 GB. SRAM-resident execution removes that, and every part is U.S.-fabbed and U.S.-packaged.

title: Watershed upstream retention: delete deep packet-buffer DRAM from switches
idea: Floodplains and wetlands hold water upstream, so the main channel needs no giant reservoir. A receiver-driven credit transport, where each host sends only the bytes it has been granted, keeps queues at the sources. Spine and DCI switches can then drop their off-chip HBM/DRAM deep buffers and run on on-die SRAM alone, with the switch ASIC fabbed at Intel 18A (Arizona) or GF Malta.
why: Deep-buffer line cards carry 8-32 GB of HBM/DRAM each. Source pacing removes that memory and designs out HBM, which has no U.S. source.

title: Seismograph-triggered camera buffers: keep only tiles whose STA/LTA jumps
idea: A seismograph records only when the ratio of short-term to long-term average amplitude crosses a trigger. A readout ASIC built on SkyWater's Minnesota 130 nm line, paired with domestically fabbed CMOS image sensors, computes per-tile STA/LTA on the fly and forwards only triggered tiles plus a low-rate keyframe into the DRAM ring buffers of ADAS, robot and surveillance systems.
why: Camera pipelines hold seconds of full frames per sensor, GBs per vehicle. Trigger gating cuts frame-buffer DRAM 5-20x, and bandwidth with it, using domestic parts from sensor to ASIC.

title: Magnetite-remanence code: execute in place from Arizona-made MRAM
idea: Magnetite in cooling lava locks in the magnetic field permanently. Edge Linux boxes, routers and PLCs put kernel text, binaries, read-only data and lookup tables in Everspin MRAM (Chandler, AZ) on an xSPI/DDR-class interface and execute them in place. Nothing is copied into the page cache, and DRAM holds only mutable state.
why: In embedded and edge systems, code plus read-only data is 30-60% of RAM. Execute-in-place from U.S. MRAM cuts DRAM per device by that much and also survives power loss.

title: Well-graded DIMM population: mixed capacities interleaved like dense soils
idea: A well-graded soil of mixed grain sizes packs tighter than uniform sand. A memory-controller interleave scheme (U.S.-designed IP on Intel 18A) uses a remap table to stripe DIMMs of different capacities across channels at fine granularity, so servers can be built in 8 GB steps (for example 16+24+32 GB mixes of Micron Manassas parts) instead of power-of-two jumps.
why: Uniform-population rules force 15-40% overbuy whenever need lands just above a step. Graded population trims fleet DRAM ~10-20% using all-domestic parts.

title: Thalweg scheduling: parallel runtimes follow the river's deepest single path
idea: A river's thalweg is its single deepest line. Parallel runtimes replace breadth-hungry work-stealing with depth-first-priority (PDF) scheduling that stays close to serial order, which bounds peak memory at S1 + O(P*D) instead of up to P*S1. It ships as a drop-in TBB/Rayon/ForkJoin scheduler for all-domestic servers (Intel Arizona CPUs, Micron DRAM) that have no HBM or U.S. NAND tier to spill into.
why: On 128-288-core sockets, work-stealing fans out live intermediate data. Space-bounded scheduling cuts parallel peak heap 2-10x for divide-and-conquer and graph codes.

title: Moraine version retention: keep MVCC versions only where snapshots paused
idea: A retreating glacier leaves ridges only where it paused. An in-memory MVCC engine keeps, for each row, only the versions visible to some live snapshot timestamp (interval GC) and deletes the versions in between, which the oldest-transaction watermark would otherwise pin. It is built into a U.S.-developed HTAP engine for servers made only from U.S.-fabbed CPUs and Micron Virginia/Idaho DRAM.
why: A single long analytic transaction can pin GBs of version chains. Interval retention cuts version memory ~10x under mixed workloads.

title: Garbage-patch sweeper: cap gyre collections where leaked objects accumulate
idea: Ocean gyres collect debris that never leaves. An agent in U.S.-maintained JVM/CPython/Go builds for domestic-only fleets uses sampled read barriers to find collections whose size grows steadily while their entries are almost never read again. It hot-patches each one to a bounded variant (cap plus LRU) and reports the allocation site to its owner.
why: Unbounded memo caches, listener lists and metric-label maps commonly leak 5-20% of a long-lived service's heap. Automatically capping the gyres returns that memory without restarts.

title: Coral per-core state: polyps share one skeleton, threads share CPU slots
idea: Coral polyps share one skeleton instead of each growing its own. Per-thread replicas that scale with thread count (allocator caches, counters, stats arrays, log buffers) move to per-CPU slots updated with restartable sequences (rseq). State then scales with 128-288 cores instead of 5,000 threads, implemented in U.S.-maintained runtime libraries for domestic Intel 18A Xeon fleets.
why: Thread-heavy services carry hundreds of MB to several GB of per-thread replicas. Per-core slots cut that 10-40x.

title: Glacial-erratic messaging: move payload boulders intact between actor heaps
idea: Glaciers carry erratic boulders hundreds of kilometers intact. Actor and message-passing runtimes (BEAM, Akka, Python multiprocessing queues) transfer ownership of a message payload by remapping a sealed region into the receiver's heap instead of copying it, and linear-type checks stop the sender from reusing it. This lets all-domestic servers, with no imported HBM and no NAND tier, run high-fan-out services in less DRAM.
why: Copy-on-send duplicates every in-flight message, and fan-out multiplies the copies. Ownership transfer cuts message memory 2-Nx in high-fan-out systems.

title: Hydrologic-cycle caching: each block lives in exactly one reservoir
idea: A water molecule sits in a cloud, a river or an aquifer, never in all three. The application cache, database buffer pool and OS page cache exchange residency hints so each block is cached only in the layer nearest its consumer, and a block evicted from an upper layer is demoted to the next layer down instead of being duplicated. This targets hosts built entirely from U.S. parts, which have no domestic NAND for a flash cache tier and so cannot afford duplicates in DRAM.
why: Inclusive caching stacks hold the same hot data 2-4 times. Exclusivity frees 30-60% of caching DRAM on database hosts.

title: Hogback index pruning: let soft postings erode, keep resistant ridges
idea: Differential erosion leaves only the resistant ridges (hogbacks) standing. An in-memory search index drops every posting whose impact score (term weight x document prior) falls below a per-term threshold, keeping only the ridges that ever reach the top-k. Rare deep queries fall back to rebuilding from the source corpus. This serves a CPU-only search tier on Intel Arizona Xeons and Micron DRAM.
why: Static impact pruning removes 50-70% of postings with negligible top-10 quality loss, roughly halving search-serving DRAM.

title: Drainage-basin vector index: one downstream link replaces dense neighbor lists
idea: A river network reaches every point with about one outflow link per cell. An approximate-nearest-neighbor index replaces HNSW's 32-64 neighbor links per vector with a drainage tree: each vector stores one downstream link to a coarser representative plus 2-3 lateral 'distributary' links to siblings, and search climbs to a basin, then descends. It runs on a domestic CPU-only vector service (Intel Arizona Xeons, Micron DRAM).
why: For compact quantized vectors, HNSW links can exceed the vector payload itself. Drainage links cut index overhead ~8-10x, fitting several times more vectors per GB.

title: Tributary messaging: MPI rank buffers merge before the main channel
idea: Tributaries merge into one channel before they reach the sea. MPI and RDMA runtimes stop keeping eager buffers and queue pairs for every remote rank; instead, one leader per node aggregates small inter-node messages, so buffer memory scales with node count rather than rank count. The target is U.S.-assembled HPC nodes with U.S.-fabbed CPUs and Micron DRAM.
why: At 100k-1M ranks, per-peer buffers consume GBs per node. Tributary aggregation cuts that 50-200x.

title: Spillway model cascades: small outlet daily, big model only for floods
idea: A dam passes normal flow through a small outlet and opens the spillway only in a flood. Inference serving sends every request first to a small model on U.S.-fabbed CPUs (Intel 18A Xeons with matrix engines) and escalates only low-confidence requests, so the large model, on accelerators fabbed and packaged in the U.S., needs replicas sized for just the 10-20% of traffic that escalates.
why: Large-model replicas, each holding 100s of GB of HBM/DRAM, scale with traffic. Cascading cuts their count 3-5x, and with it most of the inference memory.

title: Endorheic car memory: zonal ECUs drain into one domestic DRAM basin
idea: An endorheic basin drains all its streams into one lake. U.S. automakers collapse infotainment, ADAS, instrument-cluster and telematics DRAM, today each ECU provisioned for its own peak, into one zonal compute node with a single partitioned pool of Micron Manassas automotive DRAM. Hypervisor partitions give each function a guaranteed floor and a share of an elastic remainder.
why: Cars carry tens of GB spread across ECUs sized for separate peaks. Pooling cuts per-vehicle DRAM ~30-40% on an all-domestic supply chain.

title: Ocean heat-content statistics: keep ensemble integrals, not every member
idea: The ocean remembers integrated heat, not each day's sunshine. Ensemble climate, Monte Carlo risk and uncertainty-quantification codes stop holding every member or path in memory just to compute spread. Instead, members stream as they finish into per-cell Welford/Chan accumulators for means, variances and selected covariances. These codes run on national-lab nodes with U.S.-fabbed CPUs and Micron DRAM.
why: Memory falls from O(members x state) to O(state), 20-100x for 50-1,000-member ensembles, so large ensembles fit domestic nodes without HBM.

title: Octahedral reduced-grid tensors: stop storing redundant polar pixels
idea: Weather centers moved to reduced Gaussian and octahedral grids that keep fewer longitudes near the poles. Global weather and climate AI models, 360-degree video and panoramic perception store and process spherical fields on reduced grids (row length proportional to cos latitude) with ragged-tensor kernels, instead of equirectangular arrays that oversample the poles. They run on accelerators fabbed in Arizona.
why: Equirectangular grids waste ~30-36% of their points. Reduced grids cut input, activation and frame memory by that much in spherical workloads.

title: Mixed-layer sizing: cap each container at its working-set thermocline
idea: Oceanographers locate the mixed-layer depth where temperature suddenly drops. A node agent estimates each container's reuse-distance histogram online with spatially sampled page-access tracking (SHARDS-style) and sets its cgroup limit at the thermocline knee of its miss-ratio curve plus a margin. It ships in the node agent for an all-U.S. server stack (Intel Arizona CPUs, Micron DRAM).
why: Containers are typically given 1.5-3x their working set. Knee-based limits recover 20-40% of committed DRAM.

title: Catalytic scratch: borrow memory that is full AND free
idea: Kernels needing workspace (sort buffers, GEMM/attention scratch, FFT temporaries) borrow pages already holding other live read-only data (page cache, frozen weights) and touch them only with reversible XOR/modular-add updates, then uncompute so every byte returns bit-exactly to its original value, as in catalytic-space computing. A per-page 'catalytic lease' bit in the memory controller briefly stalls or redirects foreign readers to a compressed shadow while the lease is open.
why: Workspace is ~10-30% of accelerator and database memory; leasing it from already-occupied pages removes most dedicated scratch, ~1.1-1.4x effective capacity with no data loss.

title: Encoder-blind syndrome pages: store the errors, not the data
idea: Pages likely to have a near-twin somewhere (sibling VM images, successive checkpoints, replica shards) are stored only as an LDPC syndrome of ~15-25% of their size, computed locally with no reference lookup. On read, a belief-propagation decoder uses whatever similar page is resident as noisy side information (Slepian-Wolf/Wyner-Ziv), so the page is absent AND recoverable and its reference is chosen at read time, not write time.
why: Captures near-duplicate savings (3-6x on such pages) that exact dedup misses, with no fingerprint-index DRAM and no cross-node content comparison at write time.

title: Lossy AND bit-exact: Freivalds-certified 3-bit weights with flash fallback
idea: Serve from 3-bit resident weights while keeping, per matrix, a few exact random projections r^T W (one n-vector each); every step measures the true projected output error r^T(W - Wq)x on the live input, and when the top-1 logit margin exceeds the certified error the token matches FP16 decoding with probability 1-delta. Only low-margin steps rerun with exact weight blocks fetched from flash.
why: ~5x less weight DRAM while greedy outputs match full precision on certified steps; expected fallback under 5% of steps, so flash bandwidth stays modest.

title: Factorized joins: billion-row results held as compact products
idea: The query engine keeps many-to-many join results in factorized form (unions of Cartesian products along a variable order) and pushes filters, aggregates and group-bys through the factors, flattening rows only at the output cursor. The result is huge AND tiny: N x M logical rows occupy N + M.
why: Join intermediates dominate analytics DRAM; factorization cuts them 10-1000x on star, snowflake and graph-pattern queries.

title: Coded caching: each GPU holds different slices, XOR multicast serves all
idea: Each node in an inference pod caches a distinct 1/K slice of every popular expert or shared-prefix block (Maddah-Ali-Niesen placement); when several nodes miss different blocks at once, the switch sends single XOR-coded packets that each node decodes with the slice only it holds. Nodes hold less AND get served more, because the coding gain grows with the pod's aggregate cache rather than each node's.
why: Replaces K-fold replication of hot experts and prefixes with 1/K residency at similar fabric load, cutting replicated HBM/DRAM for those objects by up to K x.

title: Empty AND full: free frames carry their own page metadata
idea: The kernel's 64-byte per-frame descriptors (struct page, 1.6% of DRAM) live in the dense array only for allocated small pages; descriptors for free frames and huge-page tails are written inside the free frames themselves and materialized on allocation through a sparse virtual memmap.
why: Recovers ~1-1.5% of all installed DRAM in software (16-24 GB on a 1.5 TB server), exabyte-scale fleetwide, with zero hardware change.

title: Different AND identical: symmetry-aligned model fleets share one centroid
idea: Exploit neuron-permutation and scale symmetries: re-basin every independently trained or merged same-architecture model in a serving fleet to one canonical hidden-unit order, store a shared centroid weight set once, and keep each model as a sparse low-bit residual from it, reconstructed layer by layer at load.
why: Fleets hosting many related but not fine-tuned variants (seeds, vendors, merges, distillations) could cut resident weights 2-4x where fine-tune delta coding does not apply.

title: Authenticated without tags: MAC-free, counter-free encrypted memory
idea: Replace per-line MACs with implicit integrity (a wide-block tweakable cipher makes any tampered line decrypt to high-entropy garbage that a plaintext-structure detector flags; already-random pages fall back to MACs) and replace per-line freshness counters and their Merkle tree with epoch keys rotated by background re-encryption sweeps piggybacked on patrol scrubbing.
why: Confidential-computing integrity metadata (MACs plus counter trees) costs ~12-25% of protected DRAM; removing it returns most of that capacity to tenants.

title: Allocated AND dead: stack lines below the pointer never write back
idea: Cores export each thread's stack pointer to the cache hierarchy so dirty lines below SP are dropped instead of written back, and the kernel unmaps stack pages below a per-thread low-water mark at context switch, so committed-but-dead stack stops occupying DRAM.
why: Servers with 10k-100k threads hold GBs of dead stack; reclaiming it saves ~2-8% DRAM on thread-heavy hosts and cuts writeback traffic.

title: Dense AND sparse: keep 5% of field samples, inpaint the rest
idea: Smooth simulation fields and feature maps keep only adaptively chosen samples (edges, extrema, boundaries) plus local gradients; reads reconstruct tiles in on-chip SRAM by PDE inpainting (biharmonic or edge-enhancing diffusion), and steady elliptic fields store only their boundary values.
why: 10-20x less DRAM for piecewise-smooth fields at equal error versus full grids, beyond transform coders on such data; relieves HPC memory per node.

title: Normalized heap: denormalized for code, normalized in memory
idea: A profiling runtime discovers functional dependencies among object fields across the heap (every Order with sku X carries the same price, currency and category) and rewrites objects to hold a 4-byte reference to an interned dimension record, database normalization applied to RAM; a write that breaks the dependency splits that object back out.
why: Catalog, order and event heaps are full of repeated field tuples; 2-3x heap reduction for such services without source changes.

title: A navigable graph with no edges: implicit ANN neighbors
idea: Replace HNSW/DiskANN neighbor lists (128-256 B per node) with 4-8 learned locality-preserving orderings (space-filling curves over learned projections); a node's neighbors are simply its +/-w positions in each ordering, so the graph lives in sort order and costs one rank per ordering.
why: Links are often more than half of an ANN index's DRAM once vectors are compressed; implicit edges cut index memory 2-5x at a modest recall and latency cost.

title: Forget most activations AND learn unbiasedly: randomized backprop
idea: During training, stash only a random sparse subset or random projection of each layer's activations, rescaled so the backward pass yields unbiased gradient estimates (randomized automatic differentiation); SGD's noise tolerance absorbs the added variance, and the per-layer sampling rate adapts to a variance budget.
why: Activation memory down 4-10x with no recomputation and no quantization, for a small increase in steps to converge.

title: Smaller AND smarter: trade parameters for test-time search at DRAM prices
idea: Set a fleet-wide bytes-for-FLOPs exchange rate from current DRAM and compute prices and, per task class, serve the smallest model that reaches target quality with verifier-guided search (best-of-N with a reward model, self-consistency), so resident weights shrink 4-8x while compute rises 2-3x.
why: With DRAM ~4x pricier, buying accuracy with FLOPs instead of resident parameters lowers cost per answer; shared-prefix sampling keeps the added KV small.

title: Writing text without remembering it: KV-free masked diffusion decoding
idea: For bounded-length outputs (summaries, code edits, structured JSON), serve masked-diffusion language models that refine all output positions in parallel over T denoising steps with bidirectional attention, so no per-token decode KV accumulates; memory is a fixed canvas buffer per request plus a cached prompt.
why: Decode-time KV, often half of serving memory at large batch, becomes a fixed buffer, trading ~T short passes for 2-5x more concurrent requests per GB.

title: Isolated AND co-resident: capability compartments replace per-tenant processes
idea: Plugin, FaaS and SaaS hosts run tenants as CHERI capability compartments inside one address space, so all tenants share one copy of the language runtime, JIT code, libraries and page tables while bounded, unforgeable pointers enforce isolation between them.
why: Per-tenant process overhead is 20-200 MB; packing tenants as compartments fits 5-20x more tenants per GB of DRAM.

title: Coherent without a directory: timestamp leases for CXL shared pools
idea: Multi-host CXL 3 shared memory drops per-line sharer directories and snoop filters in favor of logical-timestamp leases (Tardis-style): readers cache a line until its lease expires, writers advance the line's write timestamp, and no sharer list exists anywhere.
why: Directory state costs several percent of pooled capacity and caps pool size; removing it frees that capacity and allows larger pools that strand less DRAM.

title: Particles that don't persist: moment-resampled particle-in-cell
idea: Particle-in-cell and Monte Carlo transport codes stop storing billions of persistent particles: each cell keeps a handful of velocity moments, and every step draws a fresh quasi-Monte Carlo ensemble that matches them, pushes it, and re-bins it into moments.
why: Particle arrays are ~80-90% of PIC memory; at ~100 particles per cell, moment storage is ~20-50x smaller, provided resampling noise is controlled.

title: One model is guesser AND judge: self-speculative decoding drops drafts
idea: Instead of a separate draft model, the target model drafts tokens by exiting early through its own first layers with a shared head, then verifies with the full stack; the draft's KV is a prefix of the verifier's KV, so nothing is duplicated.
why: Removes the 5-20% extra weights and KV per replica that a draft model costs while keeping 1.5-2x speculative speedups.

title: Search a tree while holding one branch: depth-first thoughts with KV truncation
idea: Tree-of-thought and agent search run depth-first in a single sequence: on backtrack the KV cache is truncated to the branch point instead of keeping a beam frontier, and only short scored summaries of abandoned branches are retained.
why: Peak KV drops from width x depth to depth (5-20x less for wide searches), so long reasoning needs far less HBM.

title: Present AND absent: tokens that skip a layer leave no KV
idea: Mixture-of-depths routing lets each token use only a learned subset of layers (e.g., 50%); skipped layers write no K/V for that token, and attention in those layers sees only the tokens that visited.
why: KV and activation memory fall roughly with the skip rate (about 2x at 50% routing), with quality held by training the router.
